title: ER sketch of a gym class-booking app, with a join table added late
persona: Sam, a full-stack developer at a startup that sells gym class bookings, sketches the data model from memory before asking an agent to plan a waitlist feature, because classes have been overbooked.
topic: the booking data model, before adding waitlists
realism: Before touching a schema people draw the tables as boxes with their columns listed underneath the name, then join them with lines marked 1 and n. Drawing members-to-classes as many-to-many and then remembering it is a join table is the most common correction there is, and 'what we call it in the code' renames are typical.

steps.say: This is the booking data model as I remember it.
Members, with the usual stuff, email, name, and the Stripe customer id.

add.label:
classes
--
id
title
starts_at
capacity
coach_id

steps.say: Classes, a title, when it starts, the capacity, and who teaches it.
And members to classes is many to many, a member books lots of classes.
Which means there's a join table in between, obviously, that's bookings.
Let me shove classes over to make room.

add.label:
bookings
--
id
member_id
class_id
status
created_at

steps.say: Bookings has the member id, the class id, and a status, booked or cancelled.
Oops, didn't mean to delete that one.

relabel.label:
bookings
--
id
member_id
class_id
status
checked_in_at
created_at

steps.say: Oh, and there's checked in at, I'm fairly sure, the instructors tap people in at the door.

relabel.label:
classes
--
id
title
starts_at
capacity
instructor_id

steps.say: And in the code they're instructors, not coaches, and I think it's not really its own table, it's a user with a role, so just a user id.
Dashed because I'm not sure about that one.
And this is what I want to add, a waitlist, one class has many entries in order. Orange because it doesn't exist yet.

steps.note: capacity: checked in app code I think (count bookings, then insert), probably a race

steps.say: The thing that worries me is capacity, I don't think there's any constraint in the database for it.

steps.note: does cancelling a booking free the spot straight away?

story: each box is a table: the first line is the table name, the lines under '--' are its columns

the lines are relationships read from the first box to the second: '1 : n' means one of the first has many of the second (one member, many bookings; one class, many bookings; one instructor, many classes; one class, many waitlist entries)
he first joined members and classes directly as 'n : n', deleted that line and added bookings as the join table between them
classes was moved right only to make room for bookings
a deleted bookings-to-classes line was restored straight away with undo: it was an accident, not a change of mind
bookings gained a checked_in_at column he remembered late (fairly sure: instructors check people in at the door)
'coaches' are called instructors in the code, and he thinks they are users with a role rather than a table of their own; the dashed outline marks that he is unsure of that table
the orange dashed waitlist_entries? table and its line do not exist yet: it is the feature he wants to add
he thinks class capacity is enforced in app code (count bookings, then insert) with no database constraint, and suspects a race that causes overbooking
he does not know whether cancelling a booking frees the spot straight away
partner_should_ask_about: where capacity is enforced and what stops two people taking the last spot at once
whether a cancelled booking still counts toward capacity (status stays 'cancelled' on the row)
whether instructors are really a separate table or users with a role (the dashed box)
how a waitlist entry should become a booking when a spot frees up
